title: Other people's opinions
hook: what others think is on their side of the line; how we treat them is on ours (Enchiridion 1)

segments.voice: Yesterday: serenity, courage, and the wisdom to tell them apart. Your line was know the difference. Was there a moment you had to choose between accepting and changing? Day one hundred fifteen.

You post a photo and check it eleven times in an hour. You say something in a meeting and spend the evening replaying the face your colleague made. A relative says, at dinner, so you're still doing that job? And it rattles around in your head for a week. Of all the things we try to control, other people's opinions of us may be the one we try hardest, and have the least grip on. Epictetus put it on his list nearly two thousand years ago, and his line runs right through the middle of the dinner table. Today: other people's opinions.
screen: `CHECKED ELEVEN TIMES.` → `THE FACE IN THE MEETING.` → `STILL DOING THAT JOB?`

segments.voice: Go back to the first lines of the Handbook. On the not-up-to-us list, right after the body and property, Epictetus puts reputation: what other people think and say of us. On the up-to-us list, first of all, he puts our own opinions and judgments. That's the line. Their opinion of me: their side. My opinion, and what I do next: my side. Marcus Aurelius noticed how odd we are about this. He wonders, in the Meditations, how it is that each of us loves ourselves more than anyone else, and yet cares more about what others think of us than what we think of ourselves. Epictetus adds a sharp practical point elsewhere in the Handbook. If someone speaks badly of you, don't defend yourself; he says, in paraphrase, answer that they clearly didn't know your other faults, or they'd have mentioned those too. It's a joke, and it's also freedom. Now, the line has two sides, and the second matters as much as the first. Their opinion is theirs to think. But how you treat them is yours. Letting go of what someone thinks is not the same as not caring about them. You can let your relative's comment stay theirs, and still pass the potatoes warmly, still ask how their knee is. In fact, it's easier. When you stop trying to win their verdict, your hands are free to be kind. And if the criticism has something true in it, that's yours to use, quietly, without needing them to see you do it.
screen: `REPUTATION: NOT UP TO US.` · `MARCUS: WE LOVE OURSELVES MOST.` · `THEY DIDN'T KNOW MY OTHER FAULTS.` · `HOW I TREAT THEM IS MINE.` · then, large: `THEIRS TO THINK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let one opinion stay theirs. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one opinion someone holds of you that bothers you. A comment, a look, a silence. Notice where you feel it in your body. Then, on an out-breath, picture handing it back across the table: that's yours to think. Ask one question: is there anything true in it I can use? If yes, keep that small piece. Set the rest down. Breathe. The bell holds the time.
Other people's opinions. On their side of the line; how we treat them is on ours. Today's word.

Your line: theirs to think. Today, when you catch yourself rehearsing what someone thinks of you, say inside: theirs to think. Then turn to the part that's yours: how you'll treat them next. Day one hundred fifteen.

screen: `DAY 115 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE BODY IS ON LOAN.`

howItsDone: People who practice Stoicism often treat reputation as not up to them, following Enchiridion 1, and turn their attention to their own judgments and how they treat others.

match.prompt: which side of the line — tap the pairs.

myth: Epictetus says to defend yourself when someone speaks badly of you
he jokes: say they didn't know your other faults, or they'd have mentioned those too.
Marcus noticed we love ourselves most, yet care more what others think of us
he wonders at it in the Meditations.
letting an opinion stay theirs means you stop caring about them
their opinion is theirs; how you treat them is still yours. letting go frees your hands to be kind.

fork.setup: someone tells you a coworker has been criticizing you behind your back. what does Epictetus suggest?
options: say they clearly didn't know your other faults.
find the coworker and set the record straight.
criticize them back, so it's even.
fork.reveal: don't defend yourself; answer that they didn't know your other faults, or they'd have mentioned those too. a joke, and a freedom.

original.note: Greek: opinion, reputation, what people think of you. It gives English words like orthodox, right opinion.

trapdoor: what you thought: don't care what people think.
what it means: what they think is on their side of the line; how you treat them is on yours.
what a scholar hears: in Enchiridion 1, δόξαι, reputations, sit on the not-up-to-us list, while our own judgments open the up-to-us list.

sources.ref: Enchiridion 1 (reputation among things not up to us)
Enchiridion 33 (if someone speaks badly of you, answer that they didn't know your other faults)
Meditations 12.4 (we love ourselves more than others, yet value their opinion of us more than our own)

notes: Enchiridion 33 (the 'other faults' reply) and Meditations 12.4 are paraphrased; confirm the section numbers.
Greek δόξα and the plural δόξαι in Enchiridion 1 for reputation: confirm; 'orthodox' as 'right opinion' etymology: confirm.
Enchiridion 1's up-to-us list opens with ὑπόληψις (opinion, judgment); the script says 'our own opinions and judgments'.
